arguments.text: Unnamed strings are the template. Named arguments are values the braces can see.

arguments.name: .sep
arguments.text: Text placed between the template strings before interpolation.

arguments.name: .envir
arguments.text: Where the braces are evaluated. The default is the caller.

arguments.name: .trim
arguments.text: TRUE drops the common indent before scanning.

origin.details: This is glue with a small set of arguments. Doubling a brace inserts one brace. Use glue itself when the other glue options are needed.
origin.value: A character vector with the same length as the longest input.
origin.example:
name <- "Fred"
age <- 50
anniversary <- "Saturday, October 12, 1991"
cat(as.character(str_glue(
  "My name is {name}, ",
  "my age next year is {age + 1}, ",
  "and my anniversary is {anniversary}."
)), "\n", sep = "")
cat(as.character(str_glue("My name is {name}, not {{name}}.")), "\n", sep = "")

arguments.name: parts
arguments.text: Unnamed strings are the template. Named arguments are values the braces can see.

arguments.name: sep
arguments.text: Text placed between the template strings before interpolation.

arguments.name: envir
arguments.text: Extra names. When omitted, the caller's names are visible.

arguments.name: trim
arguments.text: True drops the common indent before scanning.

translation.details: str_glue calls glue.glue. Braces are Python expressions. Doubling a brace inserts one brace. The anniversary in the example is a fixed string, so both languages print the same date text.
translation.value: A list of strings. A missing piece is stringi NA.
translation.example:
from stringr.glue import str_glue

name = "Fred"
age = 50
anniversary = "Saturday, October 12, 1991"
print(str_glue(
    "My name is {name}, ",
    "my age next year is {age + 1}, ",
    "and my anniversary is {anniversary}.",
)[0])
print(str_glue("My name is {name}, not {{name}}.")[0])
